processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Menghai: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), usually pressed into cakes, with no ripe-style piling. A ripe version is also made under the Pasha name.
harvest_season: As usual across Menghai, spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: As with other Menghai old-tree raw pu-erh, long dark olive leaves with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden yellow when young, as with young raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Typically thick olive-green large leaves, as with other Menghai old-tree tea.
taste_profile: A distinct bitterness followed by a pronounced returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Give it a quick rinse and keep the first steeps short; the sweetness comes back after the bitter opening, so let it finish before judging.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually spring material pressed the same year, then drunk young or stored; cakes carry the year, and ripe Pasha exists too, so check which you are buying. Old-tree, middle-age and plantation leaf are priced very differently, and the label alone does not prove which you have.
description:
Pasha is a tea area in Gelanghe, Menghai County, set between Nannuo and the Bulang mountains. It is a cluster, not a single village: gardens are spread across Nangan, Laoduan and the new, old and middle villages of Pasha.

The old trees are described as well preserved and largely unpruned, especially around the old village, which carries the most reputation. The leaf is made in the usual raw pu-erh way, with sun-drying and usually pressing into cakes.

In the cup it opens with a distinct bitterness and then brings a pronounced returning sweetness. Expect makers and gardens to differ.

Buy by village and year if you can. Tree-age claims need checking with a seller you trust.
history:
The name is said to mean a mountain and a river. The old gardens cover about 1.93 square kilometres, with many trees reckoned at several hundred years old, and a protected king tree in the middle village is put at about 800 years. These ages are estimates.

One seller says the present Banzhang settlement was founded about 130 years ago by Pasha residents who moved there to grow tea; it is trade lore and little documented.
